features.name: Kraken Mare
features.description: Titan's largest sea sprawls across the north polar region as a branching body of liquid methane and ethane. Cassini views show a coastline cut by bays, islands, and drowned channels, making Kraken Mare one of the clearest places to compare Titan's methane cycle with Earth's water cycle.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Kraken Mare may contain more liquid hydrocarbons than all known oil and natural gas reserves on Earth combined.

features.name: Ligeia Mare
features.description: Ligeia Mare is Titan's second-largest sea and one of Cassini's best-studied targets. Radar observations showed that this alien sea is mostly liquid methane, with a floor likely coated in organic-rich sediment that rains out of Titan's atmosphere.

details.label: Composition
details.value: Predominantly liquid methane, with dissolved nitrogen and other organics

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Cassini radar detected echoes from the seafloor, turning Ligeia Mare into the first extraterrestrial sea sounded from orbit.

features.name: Punga Mare
features.description: Punga Mare sits close to Titan's north pole between the larger polar seas and a scatter of smaller lakes. Its compact shape helps show how Titan's polar basins collect methane and ethane into a connected landscape of seas, shorelines, and bright highlands.

details.label: Mission View
details.value: Cassini's final Titan mosaic showed Punga Mare near Ligeia Mare and Kraken Mare in the north polar lake district.

features.name: Ontario Lacus
features.description: Ontario Lacus is Titan's major southern lake, a dark, smooth basin near the south pole. Cassini used it as a key comparison point for understanding why Titan's large liquid reservoirs are concentrated in the north while the south holds only one major lake.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Ontario Lacus was one of the first Titan lakes studied closely enough to compare its shoreline and liquid behavior with terrestrial lakes.

features.name: Belet
features.description: Belet is a broad dark equatorial region associated with Titan's immense dune fields. The long, wind-aligned ridges are likely built from organic sand grains produced in the hazy atmosphere and then carried across the surface by seasonal winds.

details.label: Texture Cue
details.value: Dark equatorial terrain with repeated linear dune textures

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Titan's dunes are thought to be made from hydrocarbon grains produced high in the atmosphere and dropped slowly to the ground.

features.name: Shangri-La
features.description: Shangri-La is a broad dark terrain crossed by dune-rich equatorial plains and brighter icy islands. The Huygens probe landed on the western side of this region, linking the global map to the only surface images ever taken from Titan.

details.label: Mission Link
details.value: Huygens landed west of Shangri-La on January 14, 2005

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: The pebbles imaged by Huygens looked river-worn, suggesting methane rains and runoff had rounded them long before the landing.

features.name: Huygens Landing Site
features.description: Huygens descended through Titan's orange haze for more than two hours before touching down on a dark floodplain of icy cobbles and sand. Its images connected orbital hints of channels and shore-like terrain with direct ground truth from the outer solar system.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Huygens remains the only spacecraft to land on a world in the outer solar system.

features.name: Xanadu
features.description: Xanadu is a vast bright region roughly the size of a continent, standing out against Titan's darker equatorial dune belts. Cassini replaced earlier lower-quality coverage of Xanadu with sharper imaging in the June 2015 global map, making it one of the best visual anchors on Titan's surface.

details.label: Texture Cue
details.value: Large bright region contrasting with the darker equatorial terrain

features.name: Menrva
features.description: Menrva is Titan's largest confirmed impact crater, a broad multi-ring basin visible through the moon's haze and surface deposits. It matters because Titan's atmosphere, dunes, and methane weather quickly soften or bury many impact scars.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Titan's atmosphere burns up many incoming objects, so only the largest impacts tend to survive as obvious craters.

features.name: Sinlap
features.description: Sinlap is a comparatively crisp impact crater with a dark floor and brighter rim. Its relatively fresh appearance helps scientists judge how fast Titan's winds, haze fallout, and methane-driven erosion can disguise craters.

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Sinlap is one of the few Titan craters where Cassini could clearly resolve both the rim and ejecta patterns through the thick haze.

features.name: North Polar Lakes
features.description: Titan's north polar terrain is crowded with filled and empty lake basins carved into icy crust. Cassini found that the north holds the moon's great seas plus many smaller lakes, turning this region into the centerpiece of Titan's active methane climate.

details.label: Source Note
details.value: Broad storytelling anchor for the north polar lake district rather than one IAU feature center

details.label: Fun Fact
details.value: Some Titan lake basins have steep-sided rims and flat floors, making them look more like sinkholes than ordinary impact craters.
